title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Talk and Q&A session with students at the University of Texas on February 28, 2023
summary: Pabrai opens with Buffett's 2022 letter admission that a dozen decisions in 58 years made Berkshire, using it and Rakesh Jhunjhunwala's Titan stake to argue that patience and long holding of a few great businesses drive results. He then explains why he has largely stopped looking at picked-over US markets in favor of Turkey (Reysas, TAV Airports), describes Chuck Akre's three-legged stool, recounts his Fiat Chrysler/Ferrari selling mistake, and closes on cloning and Dakshana.

ideas.idea: Even Buffett says most of his capital allocation decisions in 58 years were no better than so-so, and Berkshire's results came from about a dozen truly good decisions, roughly one every five years.
ideas.detail: Out of roughly 80 whole businesses and 125-150 stocks Berkshire has bought, Pabrai estimates at least half were outright mistakes; his guess at the dozen winners is Ajit Jain, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, BNSF, GEICO, See's, Washington Post, Cap Cities/ABC, Coke, AmEx, Bank of America and National Indemnity. Berkshire compounded about 20% a year, roughly 3.7 million percent versus about 24,000% for the S&P.

ideas.idea: Investing is a very forgiving business: 96% of a portfolio can go to zero and you still do fine as long as you never touch the one crown jewel.
ideas.detail: Rakesh Jhunjhunwala started with a couple hundred dollars, died at 62 with about $7 billion, and half of that was Titan Industries, a 4% position he put on 27-28 years earlier and never touched despite being a hyperactive trader elsewhere.

ideas.idea: The number one skill set in investing is patience, because payoffs may come in 10, 20 or 30 years.
ideas.detail: He challenged the UT student fund for planning to sell inherited positions that prior teams put heavy horsepower into, and noted their short tenure works against long-term investing.

ideas.idea: Chuck Akre's three-legged stool is a simple, repeatable filter: great economics with high ROE, a long runway to redeploy cash flows, and high-integrity management with skin in the game.
ideas.detail: Akre, 80, manages $14-15 billion from one-traffic-light Middleburg, Virginia, and calls himself a slow learner who does one thing, unlike Buffett and Munger who are Swiss Army knives. Pabrai cold-wrote him and visited in 2022. High ROE without leverage is the hallmark of a great business.

ideas.idea: Extrapolating a business 10-30 years out is very hard because creative destruction comes from left field, as Uber did to a seemingly bulletproof airport parking operator.
ideas.detail: Wally Park at LAX had leather car dividers and high-frequency shuttles that no competitor cloned for decades; he once thought he'd buy it if it came up for sale, then Uber ended the need to park at airports.

ideas.idea: He has nothing homegrown in his philosophy; everything is cloned from Buffett, Munger, Graham, Akre and others, made possible by value investing's culture of sharing knowledge.
ideas.detail: He never went to business school and self-educated via Buffett biographies, Berkshire letters, partnership letters and Munger. He recommends buffett.cnbc.com, where he listened to every annual meeting since the mid-1990s twice, in the shower, over seven or eight months.

ideas.idea: Buffett's insight that being a businessman makes you a better investor and vice versa drew him in: investing turns the 4% of an entrepreneur's time spent on strategy into 80-90%.
ideas.detail: After a small partial sale of his IT business in 1994 left him about $1 million after tax, he grew it to about $13 million in five years using Buffett's approach, then left the company in 1999 and started Pabrai Investment Funds as a hobby for friends.

ideas.idea: He ignores macro, the Fed and interest rates entirely as noise; whether prime is 3% or 7% shouldn't matter to finding no-brainers with a large price-value gap, high ROE and long runways.
ideas.detail: Asked about themes for the next decades, he redirected to Chuck Akre's three-legged stool.

ideas.idea: The US is a heavily picked-over market with more hedge funds and mutual funds than stocks, so he now spends little time on North American businesses.
ideas.detail: Thousands of smart people plus private equity compete for public and whole businesses; sellers control timing and demand premiums. Buffett faces this with $2-3 billion a month to deploy and must decide between warts and earning 2% elsewhere.

ideas.idea: Turkey is a hated, extremely mispriced trillion-dollar economy where all foreign investors combined hold about $20 billion, and his funds alone hold about $200 million, roughly 1%.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He started visiting about five years ago (this is his fifth year) despite 80% inflation and a collapsing lira, and could not get his best friends to look at the businesses. Go fishing where the fish are, as Munger says, even if it is uncomfortable.

ideas.idea: In Turkey he only looks at businesses whose earnings are in euros or dollars or whose assets have international value, so lira collapse becomes a tailwind rather than a risk.
ideas.detail: A Turkish fruit juice exporter with 90-98% of revenue from the EU (free trade under the customs union) sees euro earnings rise as lira costs fall; the baby got thrown out with the bathwater.

ideas.idea: After decades he learned that in a whole mispriced market you should go after the highest-quality businesses rather than the cheapest ones, which the 'old Mohnish' would have done.
ideas.detail: Halkbank traded at a P/E of 0.1 because its chairman ignored Iran sanctions and the CFO was jailed at Rikers; he told his friend 'I can deal with hair, but not so much hair' and moved up to the 1x P/E names.

ideas.idea: Reysas, Turkey's largest warehouse operator, traded at a $16 million market cap against $600-800 million of liquidation value in 2019, about 2% of liquidation value, and was not a fraud.
ideas.detail: 12 million square feet of prime warehouses, 99% leased on 10-year inflation-indexed leases largely in dollars and euros to Amazon, IKEA, Carrefour, Mercedes and DuPont; he bought one-third of the company for $7-8 million, including a 5% block from Templeton dumping Turkey wholesale. Market cap is now $300-350 million against roughly $1.5 billion liquidation value.

ideas.idea: The most valuable piece of Reysas is the redeployment engine: a father and son who only invest if they get their money back in dollars or euros within two or three years, which forces them into great businesses.
ideas.detail: The father never went to college and doesn't know ROE or IRR, yet built the largest private freight rail car fleet, largest truck fleet (about 2,000 trucks), lift rental and vehicle inspection businesses, redeploying cash flows at 25-35%. Only $50 million of capital ever went in (a $40 million IPO and $10 million rights issue) and no dividends were paid, producing over $1.5 billion of value in under 15 years.

ideas.idea: TAV Airports is insulated from the lira because all contracted revenues are in euros while costs are in lira, and its Almaty airport alone is worth several billion against a $700-800 million market cap.
ideas.detail: TAV operates 15 airports, eight outside Turkey, and bought Almaty during COVID for an all-in $650 million financed at 3-4% fixed; it is the only significant airport he knows that is privately owned forever rather than a BOT concession, and should produce $150 million-plus in cash flow growing 5-7% a year. He owns about 5% and expects to hold into the 2050s.

ideas.idea: Only about 300 of more than 10,000 airports worldwide are private, and that number will grow because privatization is a win-win, as LaGuardia's transformation shows.
ideas.detail: Operating airports can be a good business if you don't overpay; most private airports run on build-operate-transfer concessions of 20-50 years that revert to governments.

ideas.idea: Per Phil Fisher, if the job is done right every sell decision is a mistake; selling is much harder than buying and you can be sloppy on selling as long as you keep the crown jewels intact.
ideas.detail: Chuck Akre's fund has about 1% annual turnover versus 70-80% for typical mutual funds. Sell candidates are only cases where you misjudged the moat, runway or future of the business.

ideas.idea: Selling Fiat Chrysler and Ferrari was one of his larger mistakes: a $60 million, 10%-of-fund bet in 2012 returned about $250 million but would be worth about $600 million had he held.
ideas.detail: Fiat Chrysler had a $5 billion market cap on $140 billion revenue (4% of sales); RAM trucks earned $10,000 a truck behind an import ban, and trucks, Jeep and minivans generated about $10 billion cash flow, with 80% of Ferrari inside. His roughly 1% of Ferrari (about $20 million of cost) is now worth about $400 million, a 20x. 'Old too soon and wise too late': do not be quick to sell.

ideas.idea: The 2009 auto task force's UAW contract cut Detroit labor costs by 70-80% and restored the region's natural advantages, but the market still saw autos and unions as terrible.
ideas.detail: Steve Rattner gave the UAW until 5 pm to sign unchanged or he'd shut the lights off; they signed at 4:45. Detroit rose originally because of iron ore, coal and Great Lakes shipping, and those advantages came back. He read the actual contract via Google before investing.

ideas.idea: Judge management by track record only and completely ignore their projections; managers are optimists who see through rose-colored glasses rather than deceivers.
ideas.detail: A long history under the same manager reveals whether they under-promise and over-deliver and whether they have skin in the game; he could not find a decision at Reysas in recent years he disagreed with.

ideas.idea: Buffett's Occidental and Chevron bets are coupon-clipping bets, 'US treasuries on steroids', because Permian fracking has 90%-plus drilling certainty and OXY pumps all cash into buybacks and dividends with no speculative exploration.
ideas.detail: Munger once said he'd love an Exxon that committed to zero further capex and paid out all field cash flows; OXY behaves that way. Munger's failure to buy enough Belridge Oil in 1977 was one of his biggest mistakes. Berkshire's size forces spreading bets, as with buying all four airlines.

ideas.idea: The brain is culled and optimized between roughly ages 10 and 20, making that the only window to truly specialize, and his childhood of helping his father's failing businesses gave him 'several MBAs before 18'.
ideas.detail: Bill Gates had 10,000 hours of coding by 18-19; Buffett read every finance book in the Omaha library by 14-15; Germany's early apprenticeships explain why China cannot uproot its manufacturing. His father went bust every three or four years from over-leverage, and at 11-12 Pabrai and his brother helped figure out how to survive one more day.

ideas.idea: For a constrained US-only student fund, look for anomalies in the $1-2 billion cap range and merger arbitrage like Microsoft-Activision, and mine Value Investors Club and Dataroma rather than looking at Googles.
ideas.detail: Running $20-30 million is an advantage because smaller names are more inefficient; a 30-50 position minimum is a handicap, since Buffett told Todd and Ted he wouldn't care if they put everything in one name. After five years and about 20 company visits per trip in Turkey he found only two investments.

ideas.idea: His answer to Peter Thiel's question about a truth most of the world disagrees with is cloning: humans have an aversion to cloning just as they do to Turkish stocks, and irrational aversions are where to go all in.
ideas.detail: Stand on the shoulders of the giants who came before rather than trying to rise on your own. Cloning has helped him in many areas, including Dakshana.

ideas.idea: Dakshana succeeded because it cloned Anand Kumar's Super 30 model, scaling from 30 kids at about $800 each to about 1,000 kids a year at about $3,000 each with a 60-80% IIT admit rate against a 1.3% base rate.
ideas.detail: He found Super 30 in a 2006 BusinessWeek article, visited the Patna slum in 2007 and offered to fund scaling; Kumar declined but blessed the copy. One alumna from a family earning $75-80 a month went from IIT Guwahati to Goldman Sachs to a Stony Brook PhD and may start at seven figures, on under $3,000 invested. Buffett reads the Dakshana annual report and requests 20 copies for family and board members.
